kept.corrected_quote: The human body needs exertion... but it shouldn't be pushed to the limit. Movement of the limbs... enables the blood in the arteries to flow freely, preventing sickness from occurring. It's like a door-pivot that never decays...

kept.corrected_meaning: Your body needs to move, but not until you are worn out. Moving keeps blood flowing and sickness away.
kept.evidence: I downloaded the raw text of zh.wikisource 三國志/卷29. Line 49 reads 佗語普曰：「人體欲得勞動，但不當使極爾。動搖則谷氣得消，血脈流通，病不得生，譬猶戶樞不朽是也。是以古之仙者為導引之事…動諸關節，以求難老。」 This matches the original character for character; that edition prints 谷氣, and 穀氣 is the traditional form. For Mair's English I used the en.wikipedia 'Hua Tuo' block quote, which cites Mair 1994 pp. 695–696: "The human body needs exertion." [Hua Tuo] told [Wu Pu], "but it shouldn't be pushed to the limit. Movement of the limbs facilitates the absorption of nutrients in food and enables the blood in the arteries to flow freely, preventing sickness from occurring. It's like a door-pivot that never decays from bugs or worms because of the constant opening and closing." The candidate matches this, and every cut is marked with '...'. The archive.org scan of Mair's book (columbiaantholog0000unse_x2v9) is a restricted lending copy, and search-inside returned 403, so I could not open the printed page myself. The English is confirmed only through the Wikipedia citation, but the Chinese source is confirmed directly. I changed only the meaning line, because 'every day' is not in the text. On the stage: the trimmed quote covers stage 1 (the door-pivot) and stage 2 (prevents sickness). Stage 3 is in the same speech, which goes on to 'seeking to stave off old age' (以求難老), and Wu Pu's 90+ follows. Keep 'arc' only if a slide shows that context or it is paired with the Wu Pu item; otherwise treat it as stage 2.
kept.safety: Safe as trimmed. The same chapter goes on to cover the warlord Cao Cao, prison and Hua Tuo's execution. Never quote past 'good appetite', and never mention how he died. Name the source as 'Sanguozhi, a 3rd-century Chinese history', not 'Records of the Three Kingdoms'. The health claim is an ancient view. Present it as Hua Tuo's teaching, not as modern proof; modern evidence supports lower disease risk from exercise, not full prevention.

kept.original: ...quiescere interdum, sed frequentius se exercere; siquidem ignavia corpus hebetat, labor firmat, illa maturam senectutem, hic longam adulescentiam reddit.
kept.corrected_meaning: Doing nothing makes you old early. Moving and working keep you young longer.
kept.evidence: Opened the LacusCurtius English page for Celsus Book I. It states the text is the Loeb 1935 edition (Vol. I, p. 43) and is in the public domain. Book I.1 reads: '...he should sail, hunt, rest sometimes, but more often take exercise; for whilst inaction weakens the body, work strengthens it; the former brings on premature old age, the latter prolongs youth.' After the leading '...' (which cuts 'he should sail, hunt,'), the candidate matches word for word. I also opened the Latin page (p. 42): '...navigare, venari, quiescere interdum, sed frequentius se exercere; siquidem ignavia corpus hebetat, labor firmat, illa maturam senectutem, hic longam adulescentiam reddit.' It matches. The footnote marker after 'inaction' on the page is not part of the text. Not in used_quotes.txt.
kept.safety: OK. 'Hunt' is trimmed out. Celsus was a medical writer, not a politician. The claim that inactivity weakens the body and exercise strengthens it is general advice and fits modern evidence, so it is not overstated.

kept.who: Hua Tuo (physician, c. 2nd-3rd century CE) and his student Wu Pu · Book of the Later Han (Hou Hanshu), ch. 82B, biography of Hua Tuo; faithful English by researcher
kept.corrected_who: Hua Tuo (physician, late 2nd century CE) and his student Wu Pu · Book of the Later Han (Hou Hanshu), ch. 82B, biography of Hua Tuo; English rendering by researcher
kept.corrected_quote: Physician Hua Tuo taught: move to keep blood flowing and sickness away, but never to the limit. His student Wu Pu did the five animal exercises and, past ninety, had sharp eyes and ears, says the old history.
kept.original: 人體欲得勞動，但不當使極耳。動搖則穀氣得銷，血脈流通，病不得生，譬猶戶樞，終不朽也。…吾有一術，名五禽之戲：一曰虎，二曰鹿，三曰熊，四曰猿，五曰鳥。…普施行之，年九十餘，耳目聰明，齒牙完堅。
kept.corrected_meaning: An old doctor said: move to stay well, but never push too hard. His student stayed sharp past ninety.
kept.evidence: Opened Chinese Wikisource, 後漢書/卷82下, biography of Hua Tuo. Every fact checks out. Hua Tuo speaks to Wu Pu (佗語普曰): 人體欲得勞動，但不當使極耳。動搖則穀氣得銷，血脈流通，病不得生，譬猶戶樞，終不朽也。 The ancients did daoyin 'to seek to make old age slow' (以求難老). The five animals are 虎、鹿、熊、猿、鳥. The text ends 普施行之，年九十餘，耳目聰明，齒牙完堅 ('past ninety, ears and eyes sharp, teeth whole and firm'). I made three fixes. (1) The original story ran about 60 words, so I cut it to 38. (2) The quoted line 'Move, and ... sickness cannot arise' was a loose rendering and made an absolute health claim, so I changed it to an unquoted paraphrase that covers both his advice to move and his warning not to push to the limit (但不當使極). (3) The old meaning line said movement 'keeps sickness away' outright, so I softened it to 'move to stay well'. The age is not independently verifiable, so the story keeps the label 'says the old history'. There is no published public-domain English translation, so the English is a paraphrase.
kept.safety: OK as corrected. Never mention how Hua Tuo died: he was executed on a warlord's order. Do not name the compiler Fan Ye, who was also executed. Cite the Hou Hanshu, not the Records of the Three Kingdoms. The sickness claim is now framed as the physician's teaching and kept moderate, not absolute.

kept.corrected_who: Kaibara Ekiken (physician-scholar, 1630-1714) · Yōjōkun (Lessons on Nourishing Life), Book 1, §117, 1713; own close translation from the Japanese
kept.corrected_quote: Work the body a little every day. Do not sit at ease for long. Every day after meals, be sure to walk quietly a few hundred steps in the garden. When it rains, walk slowly inside the house, again and again.
kept.original: 身体は日々少づつ労動すべし。久しく安坐すべからず。毎日飯後に、必ず庭圃の内数百足しづかに歩行すべし。雨中には室屋の内を、幾度も徐行すべし。
kept.corrected_meaning: Move a little every day, don't sit too long, and walk after meals, even when it rains.
kept.evidence: Downloaded the Nakamura Gakuen University Kaibara Ekiken Archive text (text03.html). Under 巻第一 総論上, section [117], the Japanese reads exactly as in 'original'. No published public-domain English exists, so the English is our own. I tightened it to follow the Japanese more closely: 労動 = 'work/exert', 安坐 = 'sit at ease', 毎日飯後に、必ず = 'every day after meals, be sure to'. word_for_word=false only because there is no printed English. The Japanese itself is exact. The next sentence really does say that moving morning and evening means 'without needles or moxa ... no illness' (此如く日々朝晩運動すれば、針・灸を用ひずして、飲食・気血の滞なくして病なし). Book 2 (巻第二 総論下) §201 confirms 食後に毎度歩行する事、三百歩すべし。おりおり五六町歩行するは尤よし. Two corrections to the notes: (a) 養生の道は、病なき時つつしむにあり is in Book 1 §109, not §110. (b) The 'no illness' line is an overstated 1713 claim, so leave it off. Not in used_quotes.txt.
kept.safety: Safe. It is everyday health advice from a Confucian physician-scholar, with no war, politics or royalty. Do not quote the next sentence, which claims no illness without needles or moxa; that is an overstated health claim. Do not give an exact age on the slide, because 83 versus 84 depends on the Japanese age count; 'in his eighties' is safe.

kept.corrected_quote: Mendicants, there are five benefits of walking meditation... You get fit for traveling, fit for striving in meditation, and healthy. What's eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted is properly digested. And immersion gained while walking lasts long.
kept.original: Pañcime, bhikkhave, caṅkame ānisaṁsā... Addhānakkhamo hoti, padhānakkhamo hoti, appābādho hoti, asitaṁ pītaṁ khāyitaṁ sāyitaṁ sammā pariṇāmaṁ gacchati, caṅkamādhigato samādhi ciraṭṭhitiko hoti.
kept.corrected_meaning: Walking practice makes you fit for travel, helps digestion, keeps you well and steadies the mind.
kept.evidence: Fetched the SuttaCentral bilara API (an5.29, sujato). Pali 1.1/1.3 and the English segments match exactly: 'Mendicants, there are five benefits of walking meditation. / What five? / You get fit for traveling, fit for striving in meditation, and healthy. What's eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted is properly digested. And immersion gained while walking lasts long.' The only fix is that the candidate dropped the opening 'Mendicants,' without marking it, so I restored it. The '...' covers 'What five?'. kept.corrected_who: Chinese folk saying 飯後百步走，活到九十九 (author and date unknown) and Thomas Fuller (physician, 1654-1734) · Gnomologia, No. 6251, 1732
kept.corrected_quote: A Chinese folk saying goes: 'Walk a hundred steps after a meal, and live to ninety-nine.' An English proverb book of 1732 says: 'After Dinner, sit a while: After Supper, walk a Mile.'
kept.original: 饭后百步走，活到九十九 (飯後百步走，活到九十九)
kept.corrected_meaning: Different countries, same advice: after you eat, take a gentle walk.
kept.evidence: (1) archive.org metadata for gnomologiaadagi00conggoog shows Fuller, Thomas, 1654-1734, London, B. Barker, 1732, Oxford copy. In the djvu OCR, under 6251: 'After Dinner, fit [long-s = sit] a while: / After Supper, walk a Mile.' The text matches. (2) English Wiktionary entry 飯後百步走，活到九十九 lists it as a Chinese proverb (rhyming phrase), glossed 'Walk a hundred steps after each meal and you will live a long life.' No author or date. (3) PubMed 35147898 checked: Buffey et al., Sports Med 2022;52(8):1765-87. 7 one-day randomised crossover trials, adults mostly overweight or with obesity. Light walking breaks lowered after-meal glucose and insulin compared with sitting, and did better than standing breaks. Caveat: these were frequent short breaks during long sitting, not one walk right after a meal. Corrections to notes: the 'Temperance, Employment, and a cheerful Spirit...' line is Fuller No. 4320, not 4330 (it follows 4316-4319 in the 1732 OCR). No. 4269 'Study Sickness, while you are well' is confirmed. Changed 'promises' to 'goes' so the folk saying is not presented as a guarantee. Not in used_quotes.txt; Fuller 560 and 5410 are used, 6251 is not.
kept.safety: Safe. Label the Chinese line as a folk saying; '99' is there for the rhyme and is not a health promise. If the modern study is cited, say 'short light walks lowered blood sugar after meals in small one-day trials'. Do not claim longer life.

kept.who: Wat Pho hermit statues, Bangkok, 1830s · K. I. Matics, 'Medical Arts at Wat Phra Chetuphon: Various Rishi Statues', Journal of the Siam Society 65.2, 1977
kept.corrected_who: Wat Pho hermit statues (ruesi dat ton), Bangkok, 1830s · K. I. Matics, 'Medical Arts at Wat Phra Chetuphon: Various Rishi Statues', Journal of the Siam Society 65.2, 1977
kept.corrected_quote: At Wat Pho in Bangkok, statues of hermits made in the 1830s show 'ruesi dat ton', Thai self-stretching exercises. Each figure was meant to ease a problem, such as stiff legs, sprained shoulders or dizziness.
kept.original: ฤๅษีดัดตน (ดัดตน = บริหารร่างกาย, 'to exercise the body')
kept.corrected_meaning: Thailand has its own old stretching practice for aches and stiffness, kept in statues at Wat Pho.
kept.evidence: Downloaded the Matics PDF (JSS pp. 145-152). The Siam Society knowledge-hub page confirms 'วารสารสยามสมาคม Vol. 65.2 (1977)' and gives the Thai title 'รูปปั้นฤๅษีดัดตนท่าต่างๆ'. Matics, p. 145: '18 images of hermits ... in contorted postures which portray cures for several kinds of physical suffering' and 'Each performs distinctive yogic exercises to allay particular illnesses.' p. 146: 'In B.E. 2379 (A.D. 1836)' craftsmen were commissioned to cast 'images of 80 rishis displaying massage exercises ... less than one fourth of them survives today.' p. 148: 'Most of the nine sculptures of our series manifest cures for stiffness and sprains'. Natanta 'suffers from sprained shoulders'; Thepmontho 'alleviates stiff legs and knees'. p. 149: Sumet's attitude 'is supposed to be a cure for dizziness'. The Royal Institute dictionary (dictionary.orst.go.th) defines ดัดตน as 'ก. บริหารร่างกาย'. PubMed checks: 33706066 (Widjaja et al. 2021) had 22 sedentary women aged 62 ± 1. Note they were also overweight or obese (BMI ≥ 23). At 8 weeks they beat controls on the 6-minute walk, the 8-foot up-and-go and knee strength. 29437484 (Kongkaew et al. 2018, Naresuan) pooled 7 RCTs and found flexibility +3.9 cm at 4 weeks and +8.9 cm at 8 weeks. Its abstract says 'body flexibility'. Not in used_quotes.txt.
kept.safety: Safe if royalty is kept off the slide. Matics names King Rama III as the patron, so leave the king out. Say 'meant to ease', never 'cures'. Use 'stretches', never 'pose'. If the Thai Yoga trial is cited, say it was small and in older overweight women.

kept.corrected_who: Kaibara Ekiken (1630-1714) · Yōjōkun (Lessons on Nourishing Life), Book 1 (General Principles I), §119, completed 1713 in his early eighties (84 by the old Japanese count). Japanese text from Nakamura Gakuen University's Ekiken Archive; English is our own close translation.
kept.corrected_quote: If you live long, there is much joy and much gain. Day by day you learn what you did not yet know; month by month you become able to do what you could not yet do.

kept.evidence: I opened the Nakamura Gakuen University collated Yōjōkun text (text03.html). Section [119] sits under 巻第一 総論上 (Book 1) and contains this exact Japanese, word for word.
